questions.prompt: In the Eisenhower Matrix, which type of task should you do first?
options: Tasks that are both urgent and important
Tasks that are important but not urgent
Tasks that are urgent but not important
Tasks that are neither urgent nor important
questions.explanation: Tasks that are both urgent and important carry real deadlines and consequences, so they come first. Important but not urgent tasks are scheduled, not done immediately.

questions.prompt: What is time blocking?
options: Setting an alarm to remind you of each task
Assigning specific tasks to set periods in your calendar
Blocking all notifications for an entire workday
Recording how long each task took afterwards
questions.explanation: Time blocking means reserving defined slots in your calendar for specific tasks. Reminders and time tracking are different tools.

questions.prompt: In the Pomodoro Technique, how long is a standard focused work interval?
options: 15 minutes
20 minutes
25 minutes
45 minutes
questions.explanation: The technique, created by Francesco Cirillo, uses 25-minute work intervals followed by a short break.

questions.prompt: In daily planning, what is an 'MIT'?
options: A scheduled meeting with an internal team
A minor item you handle once everything else ends
A task that you plan to delegate to a colleague
A Most Important Task you commit to finishing today
questions.explanation: An MIT is one of the few tasks that matter most for the day, so you protect time to complete it. It is not minor or delegated by default.

questions.prompt: According to the two-minute rule popularised by David Allen, what should you do with a task that takes under two minutes?
options: Do it straight away instead of tracking it
Add it to next week's plan
Delegate it to a colleague
Batch it with similar tasks later in the day
questions.explanation: For very short tasks, logging and revisiting them costs more effort than simply doing them. Batching suits longer or lower-priority items.

questions.prompt: According to the Pareto principle, roughly 80 percent of results come from what share of efforts?
options: About 10 percent
About 20 percent
About 50 percent
About 80 percent
questions.explanation: The Pareto principle is a rule of thumb that a small share of effort, often around 20 percent, produces most of the results. It is why identifying high-impact tasks matters.

questions.prompt: Why does frequent task switching reduce productivity?
options: Each switch consumes some of your allotted work hours
Switching makes the abandoned tasks less important
Each switch carries a refocusing cost that slows progress
Switching prevents you from keeping a written plan
questions.explanation: Every switch requires your attention to reload the new task, which slows work and raises errors. Switching does not change how important a task is.

questions.prompt: Which tool is best for showing fixed commitments such as meetings and appointments in your day plan?
options: A mind map of future project ideas
A document listing long term career goals
A log of tasks completed last week
A calendar with set start and end times
questions.explanation: A calendar shows when commitments occur and how much time remains. A task list shows what to do but not when.

questions.prompt: What is a key benefit of planning tomorrow's tasks at the end of today?
options: You start the next morning with clarity and fewer decisions to make
You no longer need to check your calendar the next day
You ensure that no priorities change overnight
You can avoid estimating how long tasks will take
questions.explanation: A prepared plan lets you begin work immediately without spending morning energy deciding. Plans can still change, so a quick recheck is still wise.

questions.prompt: What is a task dependency?
options: A task that you can only complete after hours
A task that cannot start or finish until another task is done
A task that depends on your mood or energy
A task that repeats on a fixed schedule
questions.explanation: A dependency links tasks so that one must wait for another. Recognising dependencies helps you sequence work so you are not blocked.

questions.prompt: What is task batching?
options: Splitting one large task into smaller steps
Giving a group of tasks to one colleague
Grouping similar tasks and doing them together in one session
Doing every task in the order it arrived
questions.explanation: Batching groups similar work, such as replying to emails or making calls, to reduce switching costs. Splitting a task is a different technique.

questions.prompt: What does the 'eat the frog' approach advise?
options: Starting the day with the easiest and quickest task
Leaving difficult work until the end of the day
Spreading tough tasks evenly across the week
Doing your hardest or most important task first
questions.explanation: The idea is to tackle your most demanding or important task early, before the day fills with distractions. Starting with easy tasks is the opposite.

questions.prompt: In SMART goals, what does the letter T stand for?
options: Time-bound
Task-based
Team-oriented
Tracked daily
questions.explanation: SMART stands for Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant and Time-bound. A deadline makes a goal easier to plan into your days.

questions.prompt: You think most clearly in the morning. Where should you place a demanding analysis task?
options: In the late afternoon when meetings end
In your morning peak hours when focus is highest
Right after lunch to build momentum
Wherever a free slot appears first
questions.explanation: Matching demanding work to your peak energy improves quality and speed. Routine tasks suit your lower-energy periods.

questions.prompt: A support analyst keeps checking email every few minutes and loses focus on other work. What is the best fix?
options: Turn off email for the entire week
Reply only to emails from managers
Check email at set times and keep it closed in between
Answer each email immediately so none pile up
questions.explanation: Scheduled email windows keep you responsive without constant interruption. Answering instantly causes the task switching that drains focus.

questions.prompt: Your tasks regularly take longer than you plan. What is the most effective correction?
options: Plan more tasks so something finishes on time
Work faster by skipping breaks
Assume fewer interruptions in your estimates
Base estimates on how long similar tasks took before
questions.explanation: This pattern is known as the planning fallacy, described by Kahneman and Tversky, where people underestimate time. Using past results gives more realistic estimates.

questions.prompt: Your manager adds an urgent task to a day that is already full. What is the best response?
options: Explain what you have planned and ask which item should move
Accept it and work late to finish everything
Postpone the new task until your plan is finished
Drop whichever existing task you like least
questions.explanation: Showing the trade-off lets your manager set the priority with full information. Silently absorbing the work hides the cost and risks missed deadlines.

questions.prompt: Which statement best distinguishes urgent from important tasks?
options: Urgent tasks always carry greater long-term value
Important tasks are those that other people request
Urgent tasks demand immediate attention, while important tasks support your goals
Urgent tasks are those that take the least time
questions.explanation: Urgency relates to time pressure, while importance relates to outcomes and goals. A task can be urgent without being important, and the reverse.

questions.prompt: Why is a short midday check against your plan useful?
options: To confirm the original plan needs no change
To adjust the rest of the day when the morning went differently
To record your hours for payroll purposes
To replace the afternoon with brand new tasks
questions.explanation: A midday check lets you re-prioritise early if the morning slipped or something urgent appeared. Waiting until the evening leaves no room to adapt.

questions.prompt: A colleague asks for a report that is urgent for them but does not support your goals, and a teammate could easily produce it. What is the best move?
options: Do it first to keep goodwill
Ignore the request completely
Add it to tomorrow's list
Redirect it to the right person
questions.explanation: Urgent but unimportant tasks are candidates for delegation or redirection in the Eisenhower approach. Doing them first can crowd out your own priorities.

questions.prompt: According to Parkinson's law, what tends to happen if you allow a whole day for a task that needs two hours?
options: The work expands to fill the time available
The quality of the work always improves
The task finishes well ahead of schedule
The task becomes more urgent over time
questions.explanation: Parkinson's law says work stretches to match the time given. Setting realistic time limits helps counter it.

questions.prompt: Which approach to scheduling recurring meetings best protects your focus time?
options: Spreading them evenly through the day
Placing them at the start of every hour
Clustering them into set parts of the day
Leaving them unscheduled until needed
questions.explanation: Clustering meetings leaves longer unbroken stretches for deep work. Spreading them out fragments the day into gaps too short to use well.

questions.prompt: Why should you leave some slots unscheduled in a day plan?
options: Because a full calendar looks unprofessional
To absorb interruptions and tasks that run over
Because a plan is only valid with free hours
To avoid the tasks you dislike
questions.explanation: Unplanned work and overruns are normal, so spare capacity keeps one disruption from breaking the whole day. It is a practical safeguard, not a way to avoid tasks.

questions.prompt: Why write tasks as concrete actions such as 'Email the budget draft to Sam' instead of just 'Budget'?
options: Longer entries make the list look more thorough
Vague entries are easier to reorder
Specific wording lets you skip estimating time
Clear actions remove the need to decide what to do when you begin
questions.explanation: Vague entries hide the next step, which encourages procrastination. A concrete action lets you start immediately.

questions.prompt: Why capture every task and request in one trusted system?
options: It frees your mind from remembering items and prevents things being missed
It increases the number of tasks you can finish in a day
It removes the need for any prioritising
It makes every item equally urgent
questions.explanation: A single trusted capture point stops tasks living only in your head or scattered across notes. You still need to prioritise what you captured.

questions.prompt: An interviewer asks how you plan your day. Which structure gives the clearest, most credible answer?
options: List your favourite planning tools only
Give general statements about being organised
Describe a real situation, your actions and the result
Recite a memorised definition of time management
questions.explanation: The STAR method (Situation, Task, Action, Result) grounds your answer in evidence. General claims and definitions do not show how you actually work.

questions.prompt: A task has been carried over to a new day four times in a row. What is the best first step?
options: Schedule it again for tomorrow morning
Find out why it is stalling, then split, delegate or drop it
Move it to the bottom of the list permanently
Work on it only when you feel motivated
questions.explanation: Repeated rollover signals a cause, such as a task that is unclear, too big or no longer valuable. Diagnosing it lets you fix the cause instead of rescheduling again.

questions.prompt: Your day runs from 09:00 to 17:00. You have a 1-hour lunch, 2.5 hours of fixed meetings and want 1 hour of unscheduled buffer. How many hours remain for focused tasks?
options: 2.5 hours
3 hours
4.5 hours
3.5 hours
questions.explanation: The day has 8 hours, and 8 minus 1 minus 2.5 minus 1 leaves 3.5 hours. Plans that ignore buffer overstate what can be done.

questions.prompt: You have 2 free hours. Task X has impact 5 and takes 2 hours. Task Y has impact 4 and takes 1 hour. Task Z has impact 3 and takes 1 hour. Tasks cannot be split. Which choice delivers the most total impact?
options: Y and Z, for a combined impact of 7
X alone, for an impact of 5
Z and part of X, for an impact of 5.5
Y and part of X, for an impact of 6.5
questions.explanation: Since tasks cannot be split, partial credit is not possible, and Y plus Z gives 7 against 5 for X. The highest-impact single task is not always the best use of limited time.

questions.prompt: You are invited to a one-hour meeting with no agenda on a day packed with deadlines. What is the best response?
options: Accept and use the time to catch up on email
Ask for the purpose and your role, then attend, send input or decline
Decline without comment to protect your time
Accept and decide on the day whether to join
questions.explanation: Asking for purpose lets you decide whether your presence adds value or whether written input would do. Declining silently or half-committing can harm working relationships.

questions.prompt: You estimate a data cleanup at 2 hours. Your last three similar jobs took 3, 3.5 and 3 hours. What should you plan for?
options: 2 hours, since this job seems simpler
2 hours plus a few minutes for breaks
Around 3 to 3.5 hours, based on your past results
4 hours, by doubling your first estimate
questions.explanation: Past results on similar work give a more reliable estimate than a fresh optimistic guess, which counters the planning fallacy. Doubling arbitrarily is not grounded in evidence.

questions.prompt: Midweek you realise you will miss a Friday deliverable promised to a client. What is the best action?
options: Wait until Thursday in case things improve
Work through the weekend without telling anyone
Deliver a reduced version on Friday without comment
Tell the client now and propose a revised date or scope
questions.explanation: Early, honest communication with options protects trust and lets the client plan. Hiding the problem or waiting makes the damage larger.

questions.prompt: An interviewer asks about a day when your plan fell apart. Which answer shows the strongest planning skill?
options: You re-ranked tasks by impact, told stakeholders what would slip, and later adjusted your estimates
You worked longer hours until all the tasks were done
You explained that your plans rarely fail
You blamed the interruptions and resumed the original plan
questions.explanation: Strong answers show re-prioritising, communicating trade-offs and learning from the event. Working longer or denying problems shows neither adaptability nor reflection.

questions.prompt: Three stakeholders each say their request is urgent and you cannot do all of them today. What is the most defensible way to decide?
options: Serve whoever is most senior
Compare deadlines and business impact, then explain the order
Take the quickest request first every time
Split your time equally among them
questions.explanation: Using deadlines and impact gives a fair, explainable basis for the order. Seniority, speed or equal splitting can leave a critical deadline unmet.

questions.prompt: Your calendar has only 30-minute gaps between meetings, yet you must produce a long report. Which approach works best?
options: Wait until you have a completely free day
Work on it only at weekends
Break the report into sections sized to the gaps and fit them in
Use each gap to start a different new task
questions.explanation: Splitting the work into pieces that suit the available slots keeps progress steady. Starting new tasks in every gap spreads effort without finishing anything.

questions.prompt: Your tasks are a proposal due at 12:00 needing 2 uninterrupted hours, a 30-minute expense report due Friday, and a fixed meeting at 13:00. Which plan is best?
options: Do the expense report first, then start the proposal at 11:00
Start the proposal after the 13:00 meeting, when you are free
Handle emails until 10:00, then write the proposal
Block 09:00 to 11:00 for the proposal and do the expense report later
questions.explanation: The proposal has the nearest deadline and the longest focused need, so it gets protected time first. The expense report has slack until Friday.

questions.prompt: Why should your daily plan be built from your weekly priorities?
options: So daily tasks advance larger goals and are not only reactive
So you can avoid planning on most days
So every day of the week looks the same
So urgent requests never need handling
questions.explanation: Weekly priorities give the day a direction, so effort goes to outcomes that matter. Without them, days are filled by whatever arrives first.

questions.prompt: In an interview, you are asked to prioritise five tasks quickly. What is the best first step?
options: Rank them by how long each one takes
Ask about deadlines, impact and dependencies before ranking
Pick the one you would enjoy most
Start with the first one listed
questions.explanation: Prioritising needs information on deadlines, impact and dependencies, and asking shows structured thinking. Ranking by length or preference ignores what matters.

questions.prompt: You work with colleagues who are eight hours behind your time zone. How should you arrange your day to collaborate and still focus?
options: Stay available at all hours so no message waits
Do all collaboration at the very end of your day
Use shared overlap hours for collaboration and protect other hours for solo work
Skip live meetings and use only chat
questions.explanation: Concentrating real-time work into the overlap leaves the remaining hours for uninterrupted tasks. Being always available fragments focus and leads to burnout.

questions.prompt: A colleague interrupts your focus block with a non-urgent request. What is the best response?
options: Drop your task and help immediately
Ask them to email it and ignore any follow up
Say that you cannot help this week
Acknowledge it and agree a time later in the day
questions.explanation: Acknowledging the request and setting a time protects your focus while keeping the relationship positive. Dropping everything breaks concentration, and refusing outright is unhelpful.
